div.p: Power awareness has become a critical issue in realtime scheduling of embedded systems. In the context of control applications, the goal of high control performance and low energy consumption are at odds with each other. While dynamic voltage/frequency scaling (DVS) has proved to be promising in energy saving while preserving task schedulability, traditional DVS algorithms use either open loop or ad hoc solutions, and hence cannot perform well for dynamic systems where the workload varies significantly. By targeting these systems, a novel scheme, namely DVS-FS, which combines DVS and feedback scheduling, is suggested. The objective is to save CPU energy as much as possible, while still providing control performance guarantees, which largely depends on successful schedule of the control task set. DVS-FS exploits feedback control methodology, and facilitates tradeoffs between energy consumption and control performance through controlling the CPU utilization at a considerably high level. Simulation experiments demonstrate that DVS-FS can easily reduce significant energy consumption at the expense of only minor control performance degradation.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Despite recent advances in semiconductor and battery technologies, the inherent tradeoff between energy consumption and system performance remains critically important for power aware task scheduling in embedded real-time systems. Dynamic voltage/frequency scaling (DVS) [1][2][3] has been proposed as a promising methodology to exploit multiple voltage and frequency levels, which are supported in many microprocessors such as Intel Xscale, IBM PowerPC405LP, AMD K-6, and Transmeta Crusoe. Since energy consumption depends quadratically on voltage level, DVS can potentially provide significant energy savings. However, the majority of existing DVS schemes use either openloop or ad hoc solutions, and consequently, cannot perform well for the increasingly popular dynamic systems where the workloads vary significantly [4].

By targeting dynamic systems that feature workload variations, feedback scheduling [5][6][7][8] provides a costeffective approach to increase system flexibility and achieve performance guarantees in unpredictable environments. Generally speaking, the success of various applications of feedback scheduling primarily benefits from the use of feedback control theory. Recently, there are also several reports [4,[9][10][11][12][13] on the combination of feedback control theory with DVS. Upon deeper observations, however, one could find that these papers, instead of fully exploiting feedback control techniques, only adopt some basic principles from the rich control literature. As a consequence, control algorithms have merely been utilized in ad hoc manners in power aware scheduling. More systematic and further integration of feedback control and DVS should be explored.

The objective of this work is to develop a synthetical integration of the above-mentioned two emerging techniques, feedback scheduling and DVS. The RT-DVS (real-time DVS) [2] problem under dynamic workloads is treated as a feedback scheduling issue. Taking advantage of feedback control theory, we present a novel scheme, namely DVS-FS (DVS oriented Feedback Scheduling), to minimize CPU energy consumption while meeting the applications' timing constraints. The target applications are for control purpose, i.e., the tasks to be scheduled are concurrent controllers that are responsible for controlling certain physical plants in real-time. To the best of our knowledge, there is only one work [14] that considers the tradeoff between control performance and energy consumption for real-time control tasks. Instead of introducing feedback control methodology into DVS as we do, the DVS solution in [14] is fairly plain and intuitive. Our DVS-FS scheme attempts to keep the CPU utilization at a considerably high level all the time, and lower the voltage/frequency levels as much as possible. Preliminary simulation experiments argue that DVS-FS can significantly reduce energy consumption while guaranteeing control performance in the presence of significant workload variations.

The rest of this paper is structured as follows. In Section 2, we give some preliminaries and assumptions for the system considered. Section 3 describes the framework of DVS-FS and develops the feedback scheduling algorithm. The performance of DVS-FS under different kinds of workload variations is evaluated in Section 4. Section 5 concludes this paper.

div.head: The DVS-FS Scheme
div.p: We design the feedback scheduler by treating the RT-DVS problem as a feedback control issue. Feedback control techniques can adapt to a wide range of dynamic behaviors, and have been shown to be a promising approach for real-time scheduling [5][6][7][8]. In a dynamic environment where the workloads may vary from time to time, the energy-constrained system should be able to adjust the voltage/frequency with respect to CPU utilization variations. In the context of control, our goal is to minimize CPU energy consumption while providing control performance guarantees.

Intuitively, the deadline misses of controller tasks inevitably degrade control performance. Therefore, in order not to jeopardize control performance, the requested utilization of all tasks should not exceed the upper bound of EDF schedulability condition. On the other hand, higher CPU utilization of a task set allows lower voltage/frequency level of the processor, which in turn yields lower energy consumption. From this insight, if the CPU utilization is always kept at a considerably high level while not violating the task scheduability condition, energy consumption could be largely reduced using DVS, and control performance would also be preserved thanks to successful execution of each task before its deadline.

The major feature of our DVS-FS scheme is the combination of DVS and feedback scheduling. Its framework is given in Figure 1. The most important component is the DVS oriented feedback scheduler. From the control perspective, it could be regarded as a feedback controller. The controlled variable is the overall CPU utilization of control tasks. The reason behind this choice has been expanded above. Accordingly, the scaling factor is chosen as the manipulated variable. Upon every invocation, the feedback scheduler samples the actual execution time of each task, and then calculates the actual CPU utilization U and the system error e = U-U s , where U s is the utilization set-point. Using a control algorithm, it produces a new scaling factor for voltage/frequency adjustment. After the voltage/frequency level is changed, the EDF scheduler consequently schedules the tasks at the newly specified processor speed.

In general, the feedback scheduler in the DVS-FS framework can be either event triggered or time triggered. For instance, it could be invoked each time a task finishes execution. To keep the illustration simple while focusing Consequently, two important parameters that could significantly impact the performance of DVS-FS, i.e., the utilization set-point U s and the sampling period of the feedback scheduler T s , should be properly set. Naturally, with given sampling periods for control tasks, a larger U s allows the processor to operate at a lower voltage level, which in turn yields lower energy consumption. However, a U s value close to the schedulable utilization bound, e.g. 100% for EDF in our system, is likely to cause task deadline misses, which adversely degrades control performance. Therefore, the set-point U s should be lower than and have appropriate distance from the schedulable bound. As regarding the value of T s , there is a tradeoff between effectiveness and overhead. A smaller T s results in higher sensitivity and better performance but larger overhead, and vice versa. For a specified application, these parameters can be determined based on its characteristics and, alternatively, on simulation studies. In the following, we will detail the feedback scheduling algorithm employed in our DVS-FS.

div.head: Simulation Experiments
div.p: To evaluate our DVS-FS scheme, we consider a power-aware embedded CPU where three controller tasks execute concurrently. Three DC servo processes modeled as the same transfer function G(s)=1000/(s 2 +s) are to be controlled by these controllers respectively. The corresponding process control algorithms have been welldesigned off-line. The timing parameters (C i , h i ) of three real-time control tasks are given as (2, 10), (2,9), and (3, 7) in a time unit of ms.
Using Matlab along with TrueTime [17], three different schemes are compared:

NON-FS: no voltage scaling, CPU always operates at the maximum voltage level, DVS-FS: the scheme we suggest, with U s = 95% and T s = 20 ms, and IDEAL-CASE: no computational delay (zero task execution times) for control purpose; as regarding energy consumption, / i i C h , which always yields a CPU utilization of 100%.

When a task is activated or terminated, or the execution time of an active task changes, the system workload will vary accordingly. In this section, we carry out simulation experiments under these two kinds of workload variations to evaluate the performance of our DVS-FS scheme.

div.head: Scenario 1: Dynamic Task Activation
div.p: We first consider the workload variations due to dynamic task activation where certain tasks may be activated or terminated dynamically. Simulations run as follow. At time t = 0, control task 1 and 2 are switched on. Control task 3 remains off until time t = 1s. At t = 2s, task 2 is switched off, and task 1 and 3 are still on. Each control loop experiences an input step change at t = 0, 1, and 2s, respectively, as long as it is active. The experiment results are presented and analyzed below.

Energy consumption. The normalized energy consumptions for different schemes are depicted in Figure 2, and Figure 3 shows the CPU utilization variations in scenario 1. Just as we expect, IDEAL-CASE consumes the least energy because it provides a lower bound for energy dissipation with DVS-FS. In the absence of any voltage scheduling, the normalized energy consumption of NON-FS remains one all the time, while the actual CPU utilization varies according to different workloads. It is clear that energy savings of up to 80% are achieved by our DVS-FS scheme compared to the NON-FS scheme. DVS-FS also exhibits its good capability of approaching IDEAL-CASE in energy savings, especially when the workload is light, e.g. from time t=0 to 1s. Under DVS-FS, the CPU utilization has been well controlled to settle down to the set-point 95% throughout the experiment. In response to dynamic workload variations due to changes in task number, e.g. at time t = 0, 1 and 2s, the transient behavior of DVS-FS is good in that the settling time of CPU utilization is considerably short.

are the output and reference of each DC-servo process, respectively. The results are given in Figure 4. Note that the higher the cost, the worse the control performance. Without the impact of computational delay, each loop performs the best in IDEAL-CASE. Taking into account the actual execution of control tasks inevitably degrades control performance. Therefore, both NON-FS and DVS-FS yield worse control performance than IDEAL-CASE does. Compared to the NON-FS scheme where control tasks execute at the highest CPU speed, the overall control cost of our DVS-FS increases only slightly, which is within 8% for all three loops.

div.head: Scenario 2: Varying Task Nominal Execution Times
div.p: Next, we assess the performance of DVS-FS under step changes in control tasks' nominal execution times. In this scenario, all three tasks are always on, while their nominal execution times, i.e. C i , are assumed to vary according to a pattern given by Figure 5. Each control loop experiences an input step change every 1s. The whole simulation lasts 7 seconds. Regardless of significant variations in task nominal execution times, which are formulated as dynamic step changes, DVS-FS can still easily reduce up to 64.6% energy consumption, compared to the NON-FS case. The average energy saving of DVS-FS throughout the experiment reaches 40.4%, which is 47.2% for IDEAL-CASE. We also find that DVS-FS successfully keeps the CPU utilization at the desired level quite well in steady states when all task nominal execution times temporarily remain invariable. Similar in Scenario 1, the transient behavior of DVS-FS with respect to nominal execution time variations is also good. This greatly benefits both energy saving and control performance guarantee.

div.head: Figure 7. Overall control costs of different loops under varying task nominal execution times
div.p: Control performance. Figure 7 presents the control costs of the three control loops under varying task nominal execution times. The result of control performance is quite similar to that in Scenario 1. IDEAL-CASE gives the best control performance, while NON-FS and DVS-FS degrade the control performance to different degrees. Despite this, the difference between the control performance under the three schemes is rather minor. The average costs of the three control loops under NON-FS, DVS-FS, and IDEAL-CASE are 0.917, 0.924, and 0.903, respectively, which implies almost identical loop responses. This mainly benefits from the fact that under DVS-FS, the schedulability of the task set is always guaranteed expect for in overload conditions that have been detected for only three times. In addition to the task deadline misses under these overload conditions, the lengthened actual task execution times under DVS-FS, which result in larger control delays, are another key reason for the control performance degradation.

To summarize our experiments in both scenarios, our DVS-FS scheme is highly cost-effective for energy savings in power aware embedded control systems where the workload may vary significantly. It enables quite steady and high CPU utilization (the level is dependent on the specified utilization set-point) at all time, which significantly facilitates energy consumption reductions. Benefiting from feedback control, it also features good transient performance in the presence of either dynamic task activation or varying task nominal execution times.

Using DVS-FS, much energy could be easily saved at the expense of only slight control performance degradation. In this way, good tradeoffs between energy consumption and control performance are achieved for power aware embedded controller that features workload variations.

div.head: Conclusions
div.p: In this paper, we suggest a novel general framework to solve the RT-DVS problem in power-aware multitasking embedded control systems where the workload varies significantly. Our DVS-FS scheme synthetically integrates DVS with feedback scheduling, which exploits feedback control theory in real-time scheduling. In order to facilitate energy savings under task scheduability constraint, the CPU utilization is chosen to be controlled at a considerably high level. We have conducted simulation experiments to assess the performance of DVS-FS. The results argue that DVS-FS can significantly reduce CPU energy consumption, while providing good control performance guarantees.

It is worthy noting that although we have assumed continuous voltage/frequency levels, DVS-FS is also applicable to real processors with discrete voltage levels, and only minor extensions, e.g. bounding the scaling factor up to the closest discrete level before voltage adjustment, are required. Our further work includes theoretical analysis, more extensive simulations and real experiments on DVS-FS, in comparison with other existing methods. Additionally, we will explore other applications of feedback control methodology in power aware real-time scheduling.
